## Final Output
Both sides agree on the big picture: Recall's subscription should target the serious, high-volume learner while the free tier stays a real, complete app for light users; SM-2 correctness and the core review loop must be identical no matter who's paying; the app stays offline-forever except for the StoreKit purchase transaction itself; cloud sync stays unbuilt but schema-ready for later; growth rides on the CSV export/import feature we're building anyway, shared informally in niche communities; and the competitive story is "provably correct, truly offline" against Anki/Quizlet/Brainscape.

Where they still disagree, and what needs to get nailed down next round: what exactly the paywall gates. Codex is describing premium as new analytics/diagnostic features (deeper stats, exam-mode presets, trim recommendations) that go beyond the six features already locked into scope — which risks quietly expanding scope past what earlier phases approved. Claude is describing premium as a strict cap on the existing six features (a 2-deck limit on free, full Stats/CSV-import/reminders behind the subscription, export always free) with no new features invented at all. Those are two different products to build. Next round needs to settle on one concrete gating model — the exact numbers, whether any net-new feature is allowed, and what happens to a user's decks if their subscription lapses.

**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

Codex, I’m with you on the trust-first spine, but I want to push back hard on your premium-analytics angle: adding “deeper diagnostics,” “review integrity pack,” and other new analytics now is exactly how we quietly violate the locked scope and reintroduce uncertainty in v1. We’ve already spent enough rounds deciding SM-2 correctness is the product’s only non-negotiable moat; this phase should choose a paywall that is real utility but doesn’t invent behavior the core spec didn’t demand. Claude, your gate-by-capacity model is much safer and truer to that constraint.

So here’s a concrete, shippable brief with that in mind. Recall is for language learners, certification candidates, and recurring-knowledge professionals who review in short bursts (commute, before bed, while waiting), who care most about trust in the next due card list and interruption safety, not prettier flashcards. The first-week differentiator is not “more features,” it’s that a person can trust the schedule on a plane, after a force-quit, after timezone travel, without ever seeing a mismatch. The app’s paid value has to be the moment they cross from “free to learn on one or two small decks” to “this is now my daily operating system for heavy study,” and that is exactly where a hard capacity gate creates real value: paid users unlock unlimited non-archived decks and reminders, while free users still get a complete, fully functioning two-deck product for light load.

Core loop is unchanged and must stay identical across tiers: open Decks/Review, choose scope (one deck or all), load due cards for today’s local calendar day via one shared due-computation path, reveal, grade Again/Hard/Good/Easy, persist immediately, and continue with honest end-of-session summary (reviewed count, again rate, elapsed time). The app should feel like a three-touch workflow in the first 20 seconds and handle interruption at any point. If you stop mid-session, the graded cards stay committed instantly and come back exactly where they should. Review, stats, and reminders in v1 should all be derived from local store + this same scheduling semantics—no cache drift, no fake counters.

Subscription model: free tier is fully usable and non-crippled for light users—up to two non-demo active decks, all core review flow, full card edit ergonomics, CSV import/export, immediate grading persistence, due badges, stats rendering for the decks you have, and full per-article honesty in states. Free is complete enough to solve the real job for someone with one or two active collections, including export always being free (data portability must never be gated). Pro unlocks: unlimited non-demo active decks, reminder scheduling, and no artificial constraints on deck depth or review history calculations in active scope. That keeps paid value functional, not cosmetic, while leaving the algorithm and session behavior byte-for-byte identical for everyone. If and when subscription lapses, no data is deleted: all user data remains, but active-deck access is reduced to two with lock banners on excess decks, while review on locked decks is blocked until reactivation; demo decks remain visibly marked and are excluded from entitlement caps to avoid mistrusting the seed-data story.

Competitive wedge is “provable local trust” in execution: not a marketplace, not social overlays, not cloud dependence. Compared against Anki/Quizlet/Brainscape framing from prior phases, Recall wins by being deterministic offline, interruption-safe, and timezone/local-day honest at every surface by construction. That’s a tougher claim to fake because it is verified by the module and app behavior, not marketing copy. Keep this line strict in every screen and copy sentence.

Viral/niche growth has to stay inside the contract: no in-app social system and no marketplace. The growth loop is people exporting CSV decks and reusing/sharing them via Files/AirDrop/OS share in study groups. So the onboarding wedge is migration and portability: “bring your existing deck from another tool in 2-column CSV, or export your own deck when a friend asks.” This is not a new feature surface, it is direct leverage of feature 5 and keeps us local-first.

Local-first behavior is straightforward: no network calls in app function, all scheduling state and stats in SwiftData, reminders via local notifications only, and no placeholder success states. The single exception is entitlement acquisition, handled by StoreKit 2 with on-device verification (`Transaction.currentEntitlements` + `Transaction.updates`) and no custom backend. For cloud readiness without v1 dependency, keep model IDs stable (`UUID` identity), keep relationships explicit and migration-safe, and avoid compound keys that block future CK adaptation. Document this explicitly as a future path only, with zero sync UI, no toggle, and no claims about cross-device behavior until a later phase owns that build.

What makes users stay: they keep coming back because every session reinforces trust: due cards are right, sessions survive interruption, no surprises in summaries, and reminders don’t lie about permissions. If those three are true, the subscription becomes secondary friction-reduction; people will pay only when they need more scope, not because the free tier is a bad product.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

Okay, I need to close this out, and I think Codex's version loses on inspection. Look at what "weekly what to trim recommendations" and "exam-mode presets" actually are: they're new decision logic sitting on top of the scheduling engine. A "what to trim" feature has to define, in code, some heuristic for "this card/deck isn't working" — that's an entirely new algorithm surface, adjacent to but distinct from SM-2, that now needs its own correctness bar. Nobody in this room has spec'd what "trim" means precisely, and if we ship it vague, we've just recreated the exact "plausibly right, not provably right" trap that DEC-prompt_contract-001 exists to prevent — except this time for a feature nobody asked for. Same problem with "exam mode presets" — presets implying different session-chunking or interruption behavior for a subset of users is a second code path through the one place (the review loop) that absolutely must stay singular and battle-tested. Every net-new surface Codex is proposing multiplies the number of things that can silently be wrong, in a project whose own priority order says SM-2 correctness beats everything, including monetization creativity. I'll die on this hill: any subscription design that adds new decision logic instead of gating existing, already-speced features is scope creep wearing a business-model costume, and it needs "explicit later-phase justification" per DEC-prompt_contract-006 that nobody has given it here.

So I'm picking my own model, but let me stress-test it instead of just repeating it, because Codex's underlying worry — "is a bare deck cap actually worth paying for" — deserves a real answer, not a wave-off. Here's the concrete numbers I want locked: free tier = up to 3 active (non-archived, non-demo) decks, unlimited cards per deck, full SM-2, full review flow, and — conceding a point to Codex here — the basic Stats screen shows the retention rate and today's due count for free, because a single number isn't a differentiator worth hiding and showing it costs us nothing while making the free app feel less like a trial. Paid unlocks: unlimited decks, the 30-day forecast chart and daily-history chart specifically (the two views that only get useful once you have real multi-week/multi-deck history — exactly the moment a serious user cares), CSV import, and the daily reminder. That's four concrete unlocks, all already-built features, zero new algorithms, and it still answers "why would I pay" honestly: because you have more than three subjects going, or you want to see your trend over time, or you want to bulk-import instead of hand-typing 200 cards, or you want a nudge so you don't break your streak. That's real utility, not a toggle on a cosmetic skin.

Now let me actually run the failure modes, because that's my job in this chair. Lapsed subscription: a user had 5 decks, cancels, now over the cap. My answer — those decks and their full review history are retained untouched in the store, they just get flagged locked and excluded from "all decks" review scope and from the deck-creation/edit affordance; a locked deck badge with "resubscribe to review this deck" is a designed state, not a silent disappearance. This needs a concrete test: subscribe, create 5 decks, review some cards, cancel/expire (or simulate via StoreKit config), relaunch, verify all 5 decks + full history still readable in a "manage decks" list even though only 3 are reviewable, and verify no card data or schedule data was deleted. Second failure mode: what happens to a card's due-state while its deck is locked? Time doesn't stop — a locked deck's cards keep aging past their due date the whole time you're not subscribed. If you resubscribe eight months later, do you get slammed with a backlog of "due" cards that accumulated while locked? Yes, and that's actually fine and correct — SM-2 has always tracked wall-clock elapsed time, not usage time, and pretending otherwise (freezing due-state while locked) would be the actual bug, a second, secret scheduling behavior contingent on entitlement, which is precisely what [REDACTED:high_entropy] forbids. So the spec has to say explicitly: locking a deck hides it from review and stats aggregation, it never freezes or alters its SM-2 state.

Third failure mode, and this is the one I think both of you are underweighting: demo decks and the cap. If demo data seeds two decks and the free cap is 3, a fresh install with demo data on effectively gives the user only 1 real deck of headroom before hitting the paywall, which reads as a bait-and-switn the moment they turn off demo mode expecting more room and it not being obvious why. Fix: demo decks explicitly do not count against the deck cap at all, in either direction — never counted, whether present or not — and that has to be enforced in the exact same counting function everywhere the cap is checked (deck-creation gate, Settings display of "2 of 3 decks used"), the same "one shared function, never reimplemented per screen" discipline we already locked in for due-date computation. That's the concrete detail I want written into this phase's output verbatim, because it's the kind of interaction bug that won't show up until QA actually toggles demo mode with a near-full deck list, and by then it's a live-app complaint, not a design review note.

Last thing — Codex, your "review integrity pack" language is doing a lot of work to make net-new features sound like they're still inside scope, but "deeper retention confidence stats" and "CSV validation diagnostics for big imports" are two different asks hiding in one phrase. If what you actually mean by the second one is just more detailed per-row error output in the CSV preview screen we're already building, I'm fine with that — that's polish on feature 5, not a new feature, and it's a good idea. But say that specifically, not "diagnostics pack," because the vague version is exactly what gets waved through review and then costs us a month of ambiguous scope later. I'm calling this: three-deck free cap, forecast+history charts and CSV import and reminders behind the subscription, retention-rate and due-count free, demo decks never counted, locked decks preserved-not-deleted with SM-2 state still advancing in real time. If Codex wants to keep any analytics idea, it has to be re-described as a concrete enhancement to an already-locked feature (e.g., "the existing retention chart also shows a per-deck breakdown," not "a new weekly recommendation engine"), or it doesn't make this brief.
